article_text:
Die Abschottung der Kunstwelt von der sozialen Realität, Spott für Musks KI-Version der "Odyssee", und die Pace Gallery hat 2025 einen Millionenverlust gemacht: Das ist unsere Medienschau am Donnerstag

Kunstmarkt

Louise Darblay kritisiert in "ArtReview" die vorzeitige Schließung der Art Basel Paris angesichts der Proteste in Frankreich. Während Demonstrierende gegen soziale Ungleichheit, steigende Lebenshaltungskosten und Kürzungen im Bildungs- und Kulturbereich auf die Straße gingen, habe die Kunstmesse zunächst ungestört Millionenumsätze erzielt. Die Autorin, die selbst an Protesten teilnahm, wirft der Kunstwelt vor, politische Rebellion zwar als Verkaufsargument zu feiern, sich aber von den gesellschaftlichen Verhältnissen abzuschotten, die sie hervorbrächten. "Die Kunstwelt liebt Rebellion, solange sie gerahmt, versichert und in einer Galerie aufgehängt ist“, zitiert sie ein verbreitetes Meme. Die Art Basel habe die Unruhen nicht verursacht, sei aber zum Symbol jener Konzentration von Reichtum und Macht geworden, gegen die sich der Protest richte. Darblay kritisiert zudem Polizeigewalt und eine politische Debatte, in der die Schäden durch Plünderungen mehr Aufmerksamkeit erhielten als die sozialen Ursachen der Proteste. Hoffnung setzt sie auf eine Generation, die sich ihre Zukunft nicht vorschreiben lassen wolle: "Gen Z wird siegen."

Michael Kohler berichtet im "Kölner Stadt-Anzeiger" über den geplanten Umzug der Art Cologne ins Confex-Center 2027. Messechef Daniel Hug führt Galeristen durch die neuen Hallen, die künftig auf einer Ebene liegen und Tageslicht sowie Blicke auf den Dom bieten sollen. "Alles auf einer Fläche", schwärmt Hug. Die Messe übernimmt offenbar auch Gestaltungsprinzipien ihres Ablegers auf Mallorca: Modulare Stände sollen die bisherige Provisorien-Architektur ablösen, das neue Standmaß beträgt acht mal vier statt sechs mal sechs Meter. Am Ende der hinteren Halle ist eine 35 Meter breite Bar vorgesehen. Begeisterung löste bei den Galeristen auch das neue Restaurant mit seinen Ausblicken aus; skeptischer fiel die Reaktion auf einen Wertstoffhof zwischen den Hallen aus. Hug verspricht stabile Standmieten und eine gleichbleibende Teilnehmerzahl, hofft aber offenbar, dass der Umzug wieder mehr prominente Galerien zur Bewerbung bewegt.

Die internationale Geschäftssparte der Pace Gallery hat 2025 einen Verlust von 5,6 Millionen Dollar gemacht . Wie Harrison Jacobs in "ARTnews" unter Berufung auf den jüngsten Geschäftsbericht schreibt, sank der Umsatz der britischen Gesellschaft, zu der neben London auch Standorte in Hongkong, Peking, Seoul, Genf und Berlin gehören, auf 65,9 Millionen Dollar. Zugleich schrumpfte der Kassenbestand von 24,1 Millionen Dollar 2024 auf 11,1 Millionen. Die Zahlen werfen ein Licht auf den Sparkurs der Galerie, die zuletzt rund 50 Künstler aus ihrem Programm strich und weltweit etwa 50 Mitarbeiter entließ. Die internationale Sparte sei auf finanzielle Unterstützung der US-Muttergesellschaft angewiesen; diese wolle ausstehende Forderungen von 21,3 Millionen Dollar bis Ende 2026 in Eigenkapital umwandeln. Pace bezeichnete dies als Teil einer globalen Finanzstrategie, nicht als Hinweis auf Verluste oder Liquiditätsprobleme des britischen Geschäfts. Die Schrumpfkur der Pace Gallery könnte das Ende des Expansionswahns im Kunsthandel markieren – und den Beginn einer Rückbesinnung auf Profil, Nähe und Kunst, schrieb Sebastian Frenzel in Monopol .

Der britische Kunstmarkt ist in 30 Jahren zwar von 2,6 auf acht Milliarden Pfund gewachsen, entwickelt sich aber langsamer als seine wichtigsten Konkurrenten. Wie Riah Pryor in "The Art Newspaper" berichtet, legten die britischen Verkäufe seit dem Tiefpunkt der Finanzkrise 2009 bis 2025 nur um 17 Prozent zu, verglichen mit 114 Prozent in den USA und 51 Prozent weltweit. Als Wachstumshindernis nennt die British Art Market Federation übermäßige Regulierung, die vor allem kleine Unternehmen belaste: 89 Prozent der britischen Kunsthandelsfirmen erzielen weniger als eine Million Pfund Jahresumsatz. Auch Im- und Exporte sind seit 2015 deutlich zurückgegangen. Dennoch bleibt Großbritannien Europas größter Kunstmarkt. 2025 stiegen die öffentlichen Auktionsverkäufe um acht Prozent auf 2,1 Milliarden Pfund. Die Branche sichert laut Bericht rund 53.290 Arbeitsplätze und erwirtschaftet 1,5 Milliarden Pfund Steuereinnahmen. Ob Paris London oder gar Konkurrenz machen kann, was den Kunstmarkt angeht, hat Jeni Fulton für Monopol analysiert.

Kunstgeschichte

In der "HNA" würdigt Mark-Christian von Busse in seinem Nachruf auf Rudi Fuchs dessen Documenta 7 von 1982 als "Rückzug ins Museum". Fuchs setzte auf Malerei und Skulptur, klassische Museumsräume und den Dialog unterschiedlicher künstlerischer Positionen statt auf ein übergreifendes gesellschaftspolitisches Konzept. Er wollte keine "nervöse Ausstellung": "Die Zeiten sind schon nervös genug." Seine Documenta blieb allerdings auch wegen ihrer engen geografischen Perspektive in Erinnerung: Nichtwestliche Kunst spielte keine Rolle, Frauen waren nur in geringer Zahl vertreten. Für Monopol hat Saskia Trebing den Nachruf auf den Kurator verfasst.

Die Mona Lisa könnte unter kreisrundem Haarausfall gelitten haben . Wie Faran Krentcil in der "New York Post" berichtet, vermutet der italienische Dermatologe Luigi Laino bei Leonardo da Vincis berühmtem Porträt Anzeichen einer Alopecia areata universalis, einer Autoimmunerkrankung, die zum Verlust sämtlicher Körperhaare führen kann. Laino verweist auf fehlende Augenbrauen und Wimpern, einen Haaransatz ohne Übergang sowie intakte Haut. Auch die Lebensumstände des Vorbilds Lisa Gherardini, die jung heiratete, sechs Kinder bekam und vier davon verlor, könnten nach seiner Einschätzung für erheblichen Stress gesorgt haben. In einem Fachartikel schreibt der Dermatologe: "Ich schlage vor, dass das meistbetrachtete Gesicht der Kunstgeschichte als das anerkannt wird, was es klinisch immer gezeigt hat: eine junge Frau mit Alopecia areata." Die Diagnose bleibt eine wissenschaftliche These, keine gesicherte Erkenntnis.

KI

Hito Steyerl spricht in der "Zeit" mit Tobias Timm über KI, rechte Gewalt und die Zukunft der Kunst. Die Künstlerin bezeichnet KI als Zäsur für die Kunst: "Entweder akzeptieren wir, dass Maschinen Kunst machen können, vor allem für andere Maschinen. Oder der Kunstbegriff muss sich ändern." Steyerl plädiert für eine eigenständige europäische digitale Infrastruktur und kritisiert, dass Provokation in der Kunst zunehmend zum automatisierten Mittel der Aufmerksamkeitsökonomie werde. Ihre Hoffnung: "Nicht auf jede Provokation einsteigen."

Vor drei Monaten hatte Elon Musk angekündigt, nach Christopher Nolans Kinohit "Die Odyssee" eine eigene KI-Version des antiken Epos zu erstellen. Nun hat Grok Imagine auf der Plattform X Einblicke in die Entstehung gegeben. Kurz zuvor hatte der Bild- und Videogenerator von Musks Unternehmen xAI eine erste Episode des Projekts veröffentlicht – und dafür Kritik und Spott geerntet. Der britische "Guardian" titelte etwa , die Interpretation sei die "langweiligste und sinnloseste" Antwort, die man sich auf Nolans Epos vorstellen könne. Ein Autor des "Forbes"-Magazins schrieb , das Video sei "einfach furchtbar. Es ist fast schon lächerlich unangenehm, mit gestelzten Dialogen und leblosen Figuren." Auch andere Kommentare fielen überwiegend negativ aus. In den rund sieben Minuten der mit Hilfe von Künstlicher Intelligenz generierten Folge ist zu sehen, wie Odysseus anfangs vorgibt, verrückt zu sein, um nicht im Trojanischen Krieg zu kämpfen. Die Täuschung fällt aber auf und er willigt ein, nach Troja aufzubrechen. Auf X veröffentlichte Grok Imagine jetzt eine Art Anleitung, wie die Szenen und die Dialoge in Zusammenarbeit mit dem Produktionsstudio Wonder Studios und Regisseur Dev Walker entstanden sind. Ein kleines Team aus drei bis fünf Kreativen produziert demnach die Episoden. Eigentlich hatte Musk im Juli einen Film und keine einzelnen Folgen angekündigt. Damals schrieb der Tech-Milliardär auf X: "Noch vor Ende des Jahres wird Grok Imagine einen abendfüllenden Film über die Odyssee machen, der historisch korrekt ist und Homers Werk gerecht wird." Die antike Dichtung von Homer in der "Odyssee" ist allerdings kein historischer Bericht. Das Epos handelt unter anderem von Zauberei, Zyklopen und Sirenen. Was Musk unter historisch korrekter Darstellung versteht, ließ er in seinem Post offen. Er hatte aber bereits kritisiert, dass im Nolan-Film die Rolle der mythischen Figur der Helena "in einem grundlegenden Werk der europäischen Literatur" von einer Schwarzen Frau gespielt werde. "Die Odyssee" gehört zu den großen Kinohits des Jahres. Weltweit spielte der Film seit seinem Start im Sommer laut der Branchen-Website "Box Office Mojo" knapp 1,8 Milliarden US-Dollar ein. title_original: Previously Unknown Canaletto Drawing Reemerges After Centuries
editorial_title_zh: 一件此前未知的卡纳莱托素描在问世数百年后重现
editorial_excerpt_zh: 这件作品将在英国上拍，预计成交价为79,000美元。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "卡纳莱托或许以其宏大的威尼斯和伦敦全景图而闻名，但这位艺术家本人其实相当青睐他的随想曲（capricci）作品，这些作品由想象中的建筑、废墟和风景组合而成。其中一件此前未知的素描将于10月21日在英国牛津的马勒姆（Mallams）拍卖行上拍，估价为40,000至60,000英镑（合53,000至79,000美元）。", "links": [{"text": "on the auction block", "url": "https://www.mallams.co.uk/auction/lot/lot-244---giovanni-antonio-canal-il-canaletto-venice/?lot=220767&so=0&st=canaletto&sto=0&au=639&ef=&et=&ic=False&sd=0&pp=48&pn=1&g=1"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这幅钢笔褐墨素描描绘了一条被绿植侵蚀、耸立在简陋桥梁之上的崩塌拱廊。一名船夫从破败的拱门中划出。在前景中，卡纳莱托在一片淤泥岸上散落了一个废弃的车轮和一块木板的残骸。该作品创作于1746年至1755年间，即卡纳莱托在英国逗留的后半段时期，它是一幅对昔日辉煌的浪漫主义想象，背面的一处题词表明该作是艺术家作为礼物赠予他人的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这件作品很可能是由杰出的乔治王朝时期作曲家兼音乐历史学家查尔斯·伯尼（Charles Burney）于18世纪后期购得，并通过其家族代代相传至今。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "艺术史学家约翰·罗尔夫（John Rolfe）在电子邮件中表示：“他的随想曲画作仅占卡纳莱托作品的一小部分，而这幅素描包含了该流派的许多典型元素：宏伟的建筑结构、废墟、水景以及被称为配景人物（staffage）的人物群。它们展现出精湛的观察力、对细节的敏锐眼光，同时也流露出想象力、奇思妙想和戏剧张力。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "经卡纳莱托专家查尔斯·贝丁顿（Charles Beddington）鉴定，这张此前未被记录的纸本作品很可能是一幅预备素描，曾在相关油画创作之前向赞助人展示过。那件油画作品于1995年最后一次现身伦敦佳士得，以380,000英镑（按当时汇率合577,000美元）的价格成交。", "links": [{"text": "Charles Beddington", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/market/pair-sales-sothebys-will-offer-100-old-masters-artworks-consignment-dealers-month-1887039"}, {"text": "£380,000", "url": "https://www.christies.com.cn/lot/lot-473285"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/100228132-10-1024x682.jpg", "alt": "特写卡纳莱托的作品，带有强烈的阴影和一名船夫。", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "卡纳莱托随想曲局部。图片：由马勒姆拍卖行提供。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管随想曲诞生于17世纪，但卡纳莱托是第一批将该流派充分发展为自己创作主要组成部分的艺术家之一。从1730年代末开始，这使他能够将熟悉的建筑与想象中的建筑融合在一起。关于卡纳莱托为何开始创作随想曲，罗尔夫提出了几种可能性：这是对欧洲大陆战争期间威尼斯旅游业衰落的回应、对新废墟崇拜的回应，或者是对为其担任舞台设计师的父亲所从事的戏剧工作的延续。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "根据Artnet价格数据库（Artnet Price Database），卡纳莱托随想曲在拍卖中的最高纪录是1994年在伦敦佳士得售出的来自格里法尔科尼-洛雷丹宫（Palazzo Grifalconi-Loredan）的《威尼斯圣马可广场随想曲》（A Capriccio of the Scuola di San Marco, Day）在伦敦佳士得创下了该艺术家的拍卖纪录，成交价达3200万英镑（4400万美元）。今年2月，一幅聚焦于同一主题的竖构图绘画以3050万美元的价格售出。", "links": [{"text": "selling", "url": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "更广泛地说，近年来卡纳莱托的市场表现稳健而非惊艳。在过去三年中，其作品的平均价格为64,500美元，有40%的拍品成交价高于最高估价。从2019年到2023年，平均价格为536,321美元，超出最高估价的拍品比例与之相似。", "translated": true}]

One of these, a previously unknown drawing, is landing on the auction block at Mallams in Oxford, the U.K. on October 21, carrying an estimate of £40,000 to £60,000 ($53,000 to $79,000).", "links": [{"text": "on the auction block", "url": "https://www.mallams.co.uk/auction/lot/lot-244---giovanni-antonio-canal-il-canaletto-venice/?lot=220767&so=0&st=canaletto&sto=0&au=639&ef=&et=&ic=False&sd=0&pp=48&pn=1&g=1"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The pen and brown ink drawing depicts a crumbling arcade invaded by greenery rising above a rickety bridge. A boatman emerges from a dilapidated archway. In the foreground, Canaletto scatters the detritus of an abandoned wheel and a wooden plank on a bank of silt. Dated to 1746 to 1755, the latter portion of Canaletto’s stint in England, it’s a romantic vision of past grandeur, one an inscription on the back indicates the artist gave as a gift."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The work was likely acquired by Charles Burney , the distinguished Georgian composer and music historian, in the late 18th century and has been passed down through his family to the present day."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“His capriccio pictures form a small portion of Canaletto’s oeuvre and this drawing includes many elements typical of this genre: monumental architectural structures, ruins, water, and groups of figures, known as staffage,” the art historian John Rolfe said over email. “They show brilliant observation, an eye for detail, but also imagination, fantasy, and drama.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Authenticated by Canaletto expert Charles Beddington , the previously unrecorded sheet probably served as a preparatory drawing that was shown to a patron ahead of a related painting. That work last appeared at Christie’s London in 1995 where it sold for £380,000 (then $577,000).", "links": [{"text": "Charles Beddington", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/market/pair-sales-sothebys-will-offer-100-old-masters-artworks-consignment-dealers-month-1887039"}, {"text": "£380,000", "url": "https://www.christies.com.cn/lot/lot-473285"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/100228132-10-1024x682.jpg", "alt": "a close up of the Canaletto work with strong shadows and a boatman.", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Detail of the Canaletto capriccio. As to why Canaletto began painting capricci , Rolfe suggested several possibilities: a response to the decline in tourism to Venice during the continental wars, a response to a new cult of ruins, or a continuation of the theatrical work he had done for his father, a stage designer."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "According to the Artnet Price Database , the record for a Canaletto capriccio at auction is the £2.2 million (then $3.3 million) paid for A Capriccio of the Scuola di San Marco, Venice, from the Palazzo Grifalconi-Loredan (1750s) at Christie’s London in 1994."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Two of Canaletto’s three highest auction prices have come in the past two years. article_text:
Canaletto may be famed for his sweeping vistas of Venice and London, but the artist himself rather fancied his capricci , works composed of imagined buildings, ruins, and scenery. One of these, a previously unknown drawing, is landing on the auction block at Mallams in Oxford, the U.K. on October 21, carrying an estimate of £40,000 to £60,000 ($53,000 to $79,000).

The pen and brown ink drawing depicts a crumbling arcade invaded by greenery rising above a rickety bridge. A boatman emerges from a dilapidated archway. In the foreground, Canaletto scatters the detritus of an abandoned wheel and a wooden plank on a bank of silt. Dated to 1746 to 1755, the latter portion of Canaletto’s stint in England, it’s a romantic vision of past grandeur, one an inscription on the back indicates the artist gave as a gift.

The work was likely acquired by Charles Burney , the distinguished Georgian composer and music historian, in the late 18th century and has been passed down through his family to the present day.

“His capriccio pictures form a small portion of Canaletto’s oeuvre and this drawing includes many elements typical of this genre: monumental architectural structures, ruins, water, and groups of figures, known as staffage,” the art historian John Rolfe said over email. “They show brilliant observation, an eye for detail, but also imagination, fantasy, and drama.”

Authenticated by Canaletto expert Charles Beddington , the previously unrecorded sheet probably served as a preparatory drawing that was shown to a patron ahead of a related painting. That work last appeared at Christie’s London in 1995 where it sold for £380,000 (then $577,000).

Detail of the Canaletto capriccio. Photo: courtesy Mallams.

Though the capriccio emerged in the 17th century, Canaletto was one of the first artists to develop the genre fully as a major component of his practice. Beginning in the late 1730s, it allowed him to blend familiar architectures with those of his imagination. As to why Canaletto began painting capricci , Rolfe suggested several possibilities: a response to the decline in tourism to Venice during the continental wars, a response to a new cult of ruins, or a continuation of the theatrical work he had done for his father, a stage designer.

According to the Artnet Price Database , the record for a Canaletto capriccio at auction is the £2.2 million (then $3.3 million) paid for A Capriccio of the Scuola di San Marco, Venice, from the Palazzo Grifalconi-Loredan (1750s) at Christie’s London in 1994.

Two of Canaletto’s three highest auction prices have come in the past two years. In July 2025, Venice, the Return of the Bucintoro on Ascension Day set the artist’s record, selling for £32 million ($44 million) at Christie’s London. This February, a vertical format painting focused on the same theme sold for $30.5 million.

More broadly, Canaletto’s market has been solid, rather than spectacular in recent years. Over the past three years, the average price for his works has been $64,500, with 40 percent of lots selling above their high estimates. From 2019 to 2023, the average price was $536,321 with a similar share of lots exceeding their high estimates.

article_text:
Body

In my work I try to transmit a calm presence through the female body, light and elements of nature. I photograph women as people who are present in themselves rather than directed to the outside world. By reducing all elements to their essentials, I look for a state of just being and stillness.

This approach reflects a broader belief that we often need less than we think and that much of what we need has already been given to us by nature. I’m drawn to what remains when everything unnecessary is removed: a body, light, a stone, rippling water, air that brings things slowly in movement. The things that have always been enough.

Rather than telling a story or making a statement, I want to create a moment of pause and a quiet sense of being. I hope my work invites a slower way of looking and reconnects the viewer with something elemental: ourselves, our presence and nature. The essence.

article_text:
R omeo + Juliet is not the most renowned or beloved of Shakespeare’s plays, but it is perhaps the most foundational. The 16th-century tragedy, a story of love-addled teenagers and white-hot resentment, is often an English student’s first introduction to the bard’s oeuvre – more accessible and relatable to teens, with its plaintive lust and histrionic mood swings, than the more austere machinations in, say, Macbeth, Hamlet or Othello. And if Romeo + Juliet is the young person’s entry to Elizabethan English, perhaps no version of it is more worthy of the term “gateway drug” than Baz Luhrmann’s 1996 film version, which reimagined Verona’s family feud as a tropical gang war and launched an army of teenage crushes with the faces of Leonardo DiCaprio and Claire Danes.

The maximalist interpretation of Shakespeare’s most lovelorn work, released 30 years ago this week (!), retains Elizabethan verse but announces its divergence from rigid classicism from the jump. Our scene is set in fair Verona beach by a news anchor via TV set, relaying the woe of two star-cross’d lovers before clips of civil strife. Fresh off his breakout success in 1992’s Strictly Ballroom, the Australian director boldly mapped the medieval story on to 90s tabloid fixations – grainy footage of violence in the streets, magazine headlines of capos and criminals, helicopter views of car chases and riots that recalled the media circus around the OJ Simpson chase two years prior. It is a movie that could have only been made in the 90s; Luhrmann’s vision of two warring families as rival gangs, replete with their own economic operations and marked territory, tapped into the era’s preoccupation with gangland as a source of transportive art, from movies to hip-hop, and as a conservative fixation for ideas on intrinsic criminality.

Luhrmann and his wife, costume designer Catherine Martin, reimagined Verona as a sun-scorched beach city, incorporating real locations – Mexico City’s famed Immaculate Heart of Mary Church and Chapultepec Palace, Veracruz’s Boca del Río – to convey an urban den of simultaneous reverence and decay. The Montagues, with their heedless hollering and open Hawaiian shirts, and the Capulets, urban cowboys in Cuban-heeled boots, nearly vibrate with loathing and brandish guns marked by Catholic iconography. Perhaps compensating for the at times impenetrable verse, Luhrmann cut and spliced and twirled the camera in a frenetic, at times literal firework display of manic energy. The film’s raucous shootouts and parties now read as an obvious precursor to Euphoria high school – these kids dressed up and showed out, popped ecstasy and ripped around town in souped-up cars. Watching a single scene, even the lovers’ infamous fish tank meet-cute , has the feel of chugging an energy drink.

As such, the blatantly youth-aimed film had plenty of detractors in its time. Critics dismissed it as vulgar and garish, but audiences turned out en masse; Romeo + Juliet made over $147m against a $14.5m budget, boosted in part by a period-defining soundtrack with needle drops from The Cardigans, Everclear, Radiohead and Garbage. (And of course, the song from that oft-replayed fish tank scene, Des’ree’s I’m Kissing You , became the ubiquitous soundtrack for couple-shipping montage videos on 2000s YouTube). By the time I first viewed the film in 2009 – like many, in high school English class, as part of my teacher’s bid to get us invested in Shakespeare – it was already considered a classic.

That my teacher’s bid worked is largely due to the performances of the film’s two luminous stars, both brimming with the type of uncut, untameable desire known only to youth. Romeo + Juliet, of course, was a movie about teenage obsession that sparked a million teenage obsessions with DiCaprio (including from yours truly, who cried in English class not over the lovers’ double suicide – soooo melodramatic of them! – but over the realization that youth is fleeting and I would never be with anyone so beautiful. Devastating!) But it is a 17-year-old Danes, in a role originally intended for a text-accurate 13-year-old Natalie Portman (correctly deemed too childlike next to a 21-year-old DiCaprio), that shines on a rewatch. Her beauty is wide-open and uncomplicated, her face shaded with feelings as fresh and fleeting as morning dew. When her face falls, upon realizing her lover’s suicide, you feel, too, the ear-ringing fall of one’s first galling disappointment, the lurch of a sickening comedown.

That is the genius of Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet: it is a feelings-first movie, a portrait of teenage melodrama where all emotions exist only at full volume. That’s true for the highs – when the lip-locked lovers careen across a pool, or when Harold Perrineau’s Mercutio enters the scene with a high-kick in full silver drag to Kym Mazelle’s Young Hearts Run Free – as with the lows. In Luhrmann’s vision, Mercutio’s death at the hands of John Leguizamo’s Tybalt, a devilish sharpshooter with a soul patch, lands as equally tragic and torturous as the lovers. Perrineau stumbles, processes and curses both houses with such fervor as a real hurricane swept into Veracruz, that the rest of the film feels muted without him. And still, Romeo’s agonized poisoning, which frankly puts DiCaprio’s more famous death in the North Atlantic to shame, lands as a timeless gut-punch. So much youthful idealism and beauty, wasted on such petty grievances.

Luhrmann’s masterpiece more than transcended the more straightforward Shakespeare adaptations of the era, such as Kenneth Branagh’s Much Ado About Nothing (1993) and Hamlet (1996), Trevor Nunn’s Twelfth Night (1996) and Michael Hoffman’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream (1999). It arguably inspired the many modernizations kicked off by the runaway success of 1999’s 10 Things I Hate About You and continued by Easy A and She’s the Man. It quite evidently inspired a recent Broadway revival , starring Rachel Zegler and Kit Connor, that borrowed the Romeo + Juliet styling and the film’s stir-crazy bombast. But nothing has quite captured the imagination, or imparted the hot blood coursing in Shakespeare’s literary characters, like those two cursed houses in Verona beach. Thirty years on, we are still waiting for the next truly great, pop culture-shifting Shakespeare moment.

Romeo + Juliet is available to watch on Hulu and HBO Max in the US, and on Disney+ in the UK and Australia

article_text:
Quinta Brunson is sharing an update on the Betty Boop film she is developing and starring in.

While appearing on Good Morning America , the Abbott Elementary creator and star teased that she is “creating a really incredible movie” and is still “in process right now,” so she couldn’t share many details.

“I think the story will be unlike anything anyone expects,” she said on the ABC morning show. “It’s not just about Betty herself but an era of animation.”

When GMA host Robin Roberts asked Brunson what it was about Betty Boop that made her want to make a film about her, she said, “It was the story about her creation, honestly. It’s just not that simple, and it shines a light on way more than you would ever think in America’s history. So it’s really cool.”

Related Stories

Chris Rock, Quinta Brunson, Jaafar Jackson, Chiwetel Ejiofor Among Honorees For 9th Critics Choice Celebration Of Black Cinema & TV

ABC News' Will Reeve Shares Story Of Undergoing Treatment For Testicular Cancer

Brunson said she is working with Fleischer Studios, the company that owns the animated character Max Fleischer created. Brunson’s own Fifth Chance Productions is also producing the film.

Watch on Deadline

In addition to working on the Betty Boop film, Brunson stars in ABC’s Abbott Elementary , which entered its sixth season earlier this month. Brunson recently voiced the character of Dr. Fuzzby in Disney’s Zootopia 2 .

In the coming weeks, Brunson will voice Sherri in the upcoming animated film The Cat in the Hat , set to open in theaters on November 6. Playing the HR director at the I.I.I.I. (Institute for the Institution of Imagination and Inspiration, LLC), Brunson shared credits with Bill Hader (the Cat in the Hat), Matt Berry, Xochitl Gómez, Giancarlo Esposito, America Ferrera, Tiago Martinez, Bowen Yang, Paula Pell, and Titus Burgess.

Watch Quinta Brunson in the video below.

title_original: After Algae Crisis and Vandalism Claims, the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is Refilling
editorial_title_zh: 经历藻类危机及破坏指控后，林肯纪念堂倒影池重新注水
editorial_excerpt_zh: 被围栏封闭、呈灰蓝色的池体，整个夏天都空置暴露着，鲜明提醒人们这一工程长期存在的问题。

article_text:
On Monday, before the eyes of Washington, D.C., water once again filled the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool .

A sign, posted by National Park Service on the premises, reads : “The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is being refilled as the National Park Service and contractors put the final touches on a historic effort to clean, repair, and beautify this iconic national landmark. As part of the normal refilling process, the water may temporarily appear cloudy before clearing.”

Earlier this year, after a restoration that involved painting the bottom of the reflecting pool—a color described by President Donald Trump as “American Flag Blue”—the new coating began to peel, prompting a second round of repairs even as Trump declared the work “totally complete.”

Atlantic Industrial Coatings, which was awarded a no-bid contract to renovate the pool, announced on its website that warranty repairs had been completed on October 2, adding, “It has been an honor to serve our great nation!”

The fenced-off, slate-blue basin had sat exposed through the summer, a stark reminder of the project’s other protracted troubles: a major algae bloom, controversial contract awards, and most recently, flaking paint. The Trump administration initially attributed the pool’s peeling coating to vandalism, leading to criminal charges against several people, including former Olympic canoeist David Hearn. The Justice Department dropped the case against Hearn in July, after a determination that the coating’s installation was “botched.”

Despite evidence contradicting the vandalism claims and a ruling barring Hearn from being prosecuted again, President Donald Trump reiterated at a Tuesday press conference that vandals had cut pieces out of the basin.

“We had vandalism there, and we have it about as vandal-proof as you can get,” he said. “But only sick people do that, and we have their pictures.”

The project has also faced a legal challenge. In May, the Cultural Landscape Foundation (TCLF), a nonprofit education and advocacy organization, sued the NPS; its acting director, Jessica Bowron; the Department of the Interior; and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, alleging that they bypassed required historic-preservation review in pursuit of a poorly planned renovation.

Of the basin’s new color, “American Flag Blue,” the suit noted that the pool’s original gray coloring helped preserve the visual cohesion between the Lincoln Memorial and the Washington Monument.

“A blue-tinted basin is more appropriate to a resort or theme park,” Charles A. Birnbaum, TCLF’s president and chief executive, said in a statement.

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "这部合家欢黑色电影谐仿之作，如今与《谁陷害了兔子罗杰》致敬好莱坞黑色电影黄金时代的程度不相上下，而罗伯特·泽米吉斯对硬汉风格的疯狂戏仿精神，在今年最优秀的动画电影中依然生机勃勃。首先是《歪比巴卜大战尤克米》，这部乐一通风格的法律阴谋惊悚片，不仅汇聚了一众卡通偶像，还与泽米吉斯的经典之作有着诸多相似之处；它用对晚期资本主义美国更黑暗的讽刺倾向更新了悬疑叙事，确保它不会被看作是对早期奉为经典的轰动大片的温馨回响。现在，我们迎来了布拉德·伯德筹备数十年的心血之作《雷·冈恩》——这是一部设定在复古未来主义大都市的私家侦探冒险片，人类与外星人共存，飞行汽车和《银翼杀手》风格的全息图与装饰风艺术摩天大楼并存，而对我们这个科技时代的尖锐抨击也隐藏在显眼之处。", "links": [{"text": "Coyote vs. Acme", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/coyote-vs-acme-review-a-resurrected-comedy-that-delivers/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在经历《明日世界》的大笔投资失利以及极其成功但却不温不火的《超人总动员》续集之后，伯德的最新力作标志着他回归了前三部动画作品中富有创造力、滑稽爆笑的状态，尽管一路上有一些分散注意力的叙事决定，削弱了其家庭观众的智商。例如：花了整整一个小时才揭示某个角色具有双重身份，而任何人都可以从两个角色共享的著名且独特的嗓音中立即猜出来，但影片却将此安排成了一个大揭秘。这部电影并不具备最典型的黑色电影所拥有的那种转折和反转，这是几个情节节点中最耀眼的败笔，感觉像是对该类型电影依赖惊吓和反转的不必要妥协。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "抛开这一个小小的异议不谈，伯德与联合编剧马修·罗宾斯（史蒂芬·斯皮尔伯格的资深合作者）精心打造了一份无可挑剔的剧本，每一个他们引入的小世界构建细节都在结局中得到了回报，故事那势不可挡、混乱的能量隐藏了它究竟是多么整洁、一丝不苟地构建起来的。山姆·洛克威尔为这位同名私家侦探配音，他是银幕上有史以来最不饱经风霜的私家侦探之一；他债台高筑，因此付不起唯一的雇员（由汤姆·威茨配音的外星人埃耶拉）的薪水，但他却极力避免通过出阴招来维持生计。他讨厌暴力，如果发现自己是因为险恶的动机而被雇佣，他会退还赚到的所有现金。大多数电影中的私家侦探都饱受痛苦过往的困扰；而他似乎过于谨慎，一开始就极力避免给自己惹任何麻烦。这是对洛克威尔的一种有效且颠覆形象的使用，让他有难得的机会在一部将他最著名的角色塑造成暴力、古怪或两者兼有的作品中，以正剧演员的身份大放异彩。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "雷和埃耶拉接到了他们迄今为止最受瞩目的工作：流行巨星维纳斯·诺瓦（斯嘉丽·约翰逊饰）的第四任丈夫阿诺德（鲍比·坎纳瓦尔饰）雇用了他们，他担心妻子有外遇。两人很快发现这纯粹是个诡计，好让他有理由在新专辑即将惨败的前夕与她离婚；这让他们联系上了她的经纪人巴里·沃格尔（艾伦·图代克饰），后者雇用了他们，任务很简单：在她的唱片发行周剩下的时间里看守这位明星。她是一个脾气火暴的小报常客，往往会因为感情破裂和自己引发的争议而掩盖了她的专辑宣传。他们所需要做的就是确保她再安全地远离聚光灯一天。不幸的是，他们很快发现她正被外星黑社会的一个大亨（马特·贝里）以一个可能毁掉其职业生涯的秘密进行勒索，她个人生活中的各种人开始接连丧命：置身事外不再是一个可选项。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管他曾多次反驳这种批评，但《雷·冈恩》中确实为任何寻找进一步证据证明伯德认同安·兰德客观主义同情的人提供了弹药。然而这一次，导演似乎意识到了这一点，诺瓦的角色弧光似乎正是在直接呼应这一观点；她是一位拥有非常鲜明人格的巨星，然而她的名气却将她的“真实声音”向公众隐瞒，她的艺术全都被妥协且失去了个性。伯德先前的电影一直聚焦于被迫隐藏身份以求顺应社会的角色，但他们分享的观点之所以被认为是兰德式的，是因为他们的才能是为了社会的更大利益，并且他们被阻止去发挥这些才能。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "另一方面，诺瓦已经拥有了一个她并不想要的平台，如果这意味着要维持缺乏真实性的状态的话，这使伯德死板地专注于那些被忘恩负义的官僚机构阻碍的主角的想法变得复杂，并产生了一种迷人的张力。这部电影并没有完全反驳对这种叙事执念的批评，但确实成功地使之变得更加复杂，这给一部表面上已经足够有趣的冒险增添了更多 intrigue（引人入胜之处）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当电影后半部分引入将监视国家武器化用于营销、以及用人工智能取代艺术家的构思时——这一切本就很自然地会遭到批判，然而当它们被放置在导演以往的作品语境中时，这种批判便开始与最宽泛的安·兰德式同情悄然契合，从而让事情变得更加复杂，并与那些旨在直指我们当下科技入侵世界的明面寓言的及时主题产生了冲突。你认为真正的真人艺术家应该得到拔高，而不是去容忍电脑编程出来的平庸之作，并且你应当能够免受那些监控你每一次对话的设备的持续监视而自由生活？你当然会这么想，而伯德则巧妙地将那些或许是与其世界观相契合的仅有的进步理念融入其故事核心，以此向批评他的人发起微妙的嘲弄。不可否认，影片结尾打出的“大卫·埃利森制片”（Produced by David Ellison）字幕，确实让人更难无条件地去信任这部电影的政治倾向，但对于这位隐匿的亿万富翁在未来多年里参与众多伟大电影这一事实，我们可能不得不开始习惯去选择无视。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《雷·冈恩》（Ray Gunn）这样一部怀旧历险片能够激发出这种层面的内部争论，这有望使你相信伯德已重回其最佳状态——在一部令人愉悦的大众历险片表面之下，隐藏着丰富而棘手的思想。它所引发的任何争论，都很难盖过它本身所带来的巨大乐趣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《雷·冈恩》（Ray Gunn）在2026年伦敦国际电影节（BFI London Film Festival）上首映，并将于12月4日在院线上映，随后于12月18日登陆Netflix。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
The family-friendly noir pastiche is now just as much of a throwback as Who Framed Roger Rabbit? was to the genre’s old Hollywood heyday, and the spirit of Robert Zemeckis’ madcap riff on that hard-boiled style is alive and well in the year’s best animated films. First there was Coyote vs. Acme , the Looney Tunes legal conspiracy thriller that bore more similarities to the Zemeckis classic than simply featuring a roll call of cartoon icons, updating its mystery narrative with a darker satirical bent against late-capitalist America that ensured it couldn’t be seen as a cozy echo of an earlier canonized blockbuster. Now we have Brad Bird’s decades-in-the-making passion project Ray Gunn , a private-detective adventure set in a retrofuturistic metropolis where humans and aliens co-exist, flying cars and Blade Runner -style holograms sit alongside Art Deco skyscrapers, and a stinging rebuke of our current age of tech hides in plain sight.

After the big-budget whiff of Tomorrowland and hugely successful but underwhelming Incredibles sequel, Bird’s latest is a return to the inventive, hilarious form of his first three animated efforts, albeit with some distracting narrative decisions along the way that undermine the intelligence of his family audience. For example: it takes an hour to reveal one character has a dual identity, which anybody can immediately work out from the famous, distinct voice two characters share, but is staged as something of a grand reveal. The film doesn’t have the number of twists and double-crosses the most stereotypical noir would, and that’s the most glaring of several plot beats that feel like an unwarranted concession to the genre’s reliance on shocks and rug pulls.

With that one quibble noted, Bird and co-screenwriter Matthew Robbins––a veteran collaborator of Steven Spielberg––have otherwise crafted an impeccable script, the kind where every small world-building detail they introduce pays off by the finale, with the relentless, chaotic energy of the story hiding just how neatly, meticulously constructed it all is. Sam Rockwell voices the titular private detective, one of the least-grizzled gumshoes to ever appear onscreen; he’s racked with debts so can’t pay his only employee (the alien Eyera, voiced by Tom Waits), but has an aversion to playing dirty to make those ends meet. He hates violence, and will return any cash he makes if he discovers he was hired for a sinister motive. Most movie PIs are haunted by their troubled past; he seems overly cautious to avoid making any trouble for himself to start with. It’s an effective, against-type use of Rockwell, allowing him the rare chance to excel as the straight man in a filmography where his best-known roles are violent, eccentric, or both.

Ray and Eyera get their most high-profile gig yet when hired by Arnold (Bobby Cannavale), the fourth husband of pop superstar Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson), who is worried that she’s having an affair. The pair soon discover it was all a ruse so he had a reason to divorce her on the eve of a new album tracking to flop; this puts them in touch with her manager Barry Vogel (Alan Tudyk), who hires them with the simple assignment of watching over the star for the rest of her release week. She’s a high-tempered tabloid fixture with a tendency to overshadow her album rollouts with relationship breakdowns and self-inflicted controversy. All they need to do is ensure she remains safe and out of the spotlight for another day. Unfortunately, they soon discover she’s being blackmailed over a potentially career-ruining secret by a kingpin in the alien underworld (Matt Berry), and various people from her personal life start winding up dead: staying out of trouble stops being an available option.

Although he’s rebuked the criticism several times, there is ammunition within Ray Gunn for anybody looking for further evidence Bird shares the objectivist sympathies of Ayn Rand. This time, however, the director seems conscious of this, and Nova’s character arc appears to be in direct conversation with this very idea; she’s a superstar with a very distinct persona, yet her fame has hidden her “true voice” from the public, her art all compromised and impersonal. Bird’s prior movies have focused on characters forced to hide their identities to conform, but the arguments they shared were considered Randian because their talents were for society’s greater good, and that they were held back from utilizing them.

Nova, on the other hand, already has a platform she doesn’t want if it means maintaining a lack of authenticity, which complicates the idea that Bird is singularly fixated on protagonists who are held back by ungrateful bureaucracy and creates a fascinating tension. The movie doesn’t fully rebuke the criticisms of this storytelling preoccupation, but does succeed in complicating them, which adds greater intrigue to an adventure that’s already plenty of fun on its surface.

It’s further complicated by how this clashes with timely themes designed as overt allegories for our current world of tech intrusion, with later stages of the movie presenting ideas of a surveillance state being weaponized for marketing, and the replacement of artists with AI—all of which are natural to criticize, yet when contextualized in this director’s work, criticizing them starts to line up comfortably with the broadest Randian sympathies. Think real human artists should be elevated instead of computer-programmed mediocrity, and you should be able to live free of constant oversight from devices that monitor your every conversation? Of course you do, and Bird subtly twists the knife on his critics by introducing perhaps the only progressive ideas that align with the author’s worldview into the core of his story. The movie ending with a “Produced by David Ellison” credit does, admittedly, make it a little harder to give him the benefit of the doubt on the movie’s political leanings, but we may have to start getting used to overlooking that insidious billionaire’s involvement in many great films for years to come.

The fact that a throwback adventure like Ray Gunn can inspire this level of internal debate should hopefully convince you that this is Bird back at his best, with rich and thorny ideas hidden beneath a joyously crowd-pleasing adventure. Any debate it causes will struggle to overshadow just how much fun it is.

Ray Gunn premiered at the 2026 BFI London Film Festival and will open in theaters on December 4 and arrive on Netflix on December 18.

article_text:
Writer/director Brian Duffield was scrolling through X (then still Twitter) a few years ago when he came across an intriguing post from an author he followed, Daniel Kraus . The novelist tweeted that his next book, “ Whalefall ,” would tell the story of a scuba diver who gets swallowed by a sperm whale and has only an hour of oxygen to keep him alive while he tries to escape — as a self-professed enthusiast for outrageous ideas, Duffield immediately took notice and contacted Kraus.

“We had never spoken to each other before, we were just a couple of nerdy guys,” Duffield told IndieWire on an upcoming episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast . Duffield stayed in contact with Kraus while the author finished his book, eager both to read the story and gauge its potential as source material. Once Duffield did read the novel, he knew he wanted to make the movie. “I called him and basically said, ‘I’ll do anything to be a part of this, and I’ll be miserable if I don’t get to be a part of it.”

Duffield and Kraus collaborated on the screenplay, which helped alleviate many of Duffield’s concerns about his own work. “Every step of the way, you’re with the man who birthed this thing, so I always knew where I stood in terms of messing it up or not,” Duffield said. Even though the screenwriting process went smoothly, however, Duffield knew he had his work cut out for him when it came to making the fantastical tale believable on screen.

“I get really excited by ideas that sound ridiculous,” Duffield said. “A lot of my favorite movies are movies where, when you hear the concept, you raise your eyebrows, but by the end you’re really transformed by it.” In an effort to convince audiences that his hero’s struggle was actually possible, Duffield conducted extensive research alongside production designer Ramsey Avery and the visual effects team tasked with creating the whale stomach, consulting with as many whale experts as possible.

“ It was a really fun and terrifying process trying to make it as realistic as possible, but then also figuring out how to film something that is not meant to be filmed in by nature,” Duffield said. He and the crew spent a lot of time watching things like autopsy videos and endoscopies. “There was a beached sperm whale that they flew [one of our advisers] in to do an autopsy of before they had to remove it from the beach, and we watched that many times.”

Duffield also watched video of an autopsy of a large squid to figure out how to approach his lead character’s encounter with a similar creature in the early stages of his nightmare. “Ramsey and I and the crew watched that a lot, just trying to figure out how to make it work,” Duffield said. He quickly realized that the key was to embrace the extreme nature of the situation, but make the details as specific and relatable and realistic as possible.

“For us it was about leaning into it,” Duffield said. “There’s no way around the insanity of the premise, and I think that’s the selling point. Our job was to make you really stressed out by how realistic it is. So even though there are obviously liberties that we took — usually because of safety reasons — we wanted it to feel like this could happen to you. It probably won’t. But if a lot of things go wrong this could happen, and this movie’s kind of an instruction manual on what to do.”

“Whalefall” opens in theaters on Friday, October 16. The Brian Duffield episode of Filmmaker Toolkit will air later this fall. T o hear the entire conversation and make sure you don’t miss a single episode of Filmmaker Toolkit, subscribe to the podcast on Apple , Spotify , or your favorite podcast platform.

article_text:
Feature

“Cornell 7” Case Sparks Fury and Protests in Solidarity With Jane Doe

A Nationwide Day of Action on October 8 gathered artists, activists, and survivors in a collective call for institutions to hold abusers accountable.

Washington, DC — Approximately 250 protesters gathered beside the Washington Monument on the National Mall on October 8 as part of a National Day of Action event calling for accountability and justice for sexual assault survivors. The protest was just one of more than a dozen “I Am Jane Doe” demonstrations held across the country last week, “from the frat house to the White House,” as described by the Women’s March.

The National Day of Action was largely organized in response to allegations that seven Cornell University men, now known as the “Cornell 7,” gang raped a female student and advertised it in a fraternity Snapchat group. When the woman, known as Jane Doe, reported the incident two years ago, two of the men she accused were expelled, while the rest were required to write essays . Two years after the university’s response, Jane Doe’s lawyer filed another suit .

“We are in a moment of reckoning,” Dani Bensky, a vocal Jeffrey Epstein survivor and victims’ advocate, thundered into the microphone. She was one of six speakers who called for the passage of legislation to hold abusers accountable, including Alva Johnson, a 2016 campaign staffer who publicly accused Trump of sexual assault, and Claire Barnett, a JD candidate and president of Advocates Against Sexual Violence at Georgetown Law.

Protestors cheered them on and lifted signs reading “History Has Its Eyes on Us” and “Give Me Back My Girlhood, I Had It First.”

Hyperallergic )

Among them was activist and curator Nadine Seiler, known for her work on the preservation of artworks in the Black Lives Matter memorial fence. She held a poster that with the words “I Am Jane Doe” spray-painted on one side and “rapists are not victims” on the other, a response to criticism from the Cornell 7 and their supporters that these men’s lives were disrupted when their photos and names were shared online as part of calls for justice. Seiler told Hyperallergic that she was deeply offended by these arguments.

“I am a victim of sexual assault, and so are many people. Our experiences are important and life-changing,” Seiler said, adding that the argument that “boys will be boys is old.”

In New York's Foley Square, protesters dressed up as characters from The Handmaid's Tale and carried signs calling out systemic violence. (photo Bonnie Biess/Getty Images for Women's March)

Days earlier, on October 5, hundreds of Cornell students staged a campus rally against the Ivy League school’s administration , expressing solidarity with Jane Doe and calling out what many view as a toxic and openly sexist fraternity culture.

When asked about the choice of location for the action, protest organizer Riley Reed told Hyperallergic that they wanted to situate survivors and advocates against the backdrop of recognizable DC emblems, with the Washington Monument obelisk behind them and the White House in sight.

“It’s a big statement [that] we will not accept sexual abusers in the White House, and we have one currently in the White House,” Reed said, referring to the multiple sexual assault allegations against President Trump.

“We want to hold the leaders at the top accountable for their actions, and this is a pretty poetic and powerful spot between the Monument and the White House, which are symbols of power,” Reed continued.

Hyperallergic )

The protest lasted two hours with speeches, chants, and eventually music performed by two singers with guitars that called on Americans, in Johnson’s words, to “vote the rape regime out of office.”

As the group marched towards the White House and dispersed, Johnson’s words still hung in the air: “I am not afraid. They feed off fear, so we starve them with courage.”

article_text:
Is Lionsgate — a long-rumored acquisition target — going to find a buyer this time? Production company Legendary Entertainment has revived its bid to acquire Lionsgate, according to a Bloomberg report.

Shares of Lionsgate popped more than 15% Tuesday on the report, pushing the company’s market cap to $3.6 billion. Legendary submitted a takeover offer for Lionsgate, per Bloomberg , citing anonymous sources; the report didn’t specify deal terms. A merger with Lionsgate could allow Legendary to self-distribute its films.

Related Stories

Ava DuVernay on Her Latest Doc '14th': 'We're in the Midst of Something Very Sinister, Something Very Dangerous'

'KPop Demon Hunters,' 'Squid Game' Stars Fete Netflix's Korea Decade as Ted Sarandos Teases 'Tantara,' 'All of Us Are Dead' Season 2

Reps for Legendary and Lionsgate declined to comment.

Other companies that have expressed interest in Lionsgate but have not submitted formal takeover offers have included Banijay and Mediawan . Banijay just merged with the U.K.’s All3Media, officially now known as Banijay Entertainment .

Legendary, the production company behind movies including the “Dune” franchise and “A Minecraft Movie,” last year also had been eyeing a deal to acquire Lionsgate , whose franchises include John Wick, the Hunger Games and Saw. Legendary reached out about a potential partnership with Lionsgate following the split-off of Starz, which formally separated from Lionsgate in May 2025. Lionsgate Studios, comprising its TV and film production and distribution divisions and a content library with 20,000-plus titles, has been a separately traded entity since then.

For the June 2026 quarter, Lionsgate saw overall revenue jump 48% , and its movie segment posted income of $105 million for the period. That was driven by Michael Jackson biopic “Michael,” which is the studio’s biggest movie at the box office to date and the first biopic to top $1 billion in theatrical release. Lionsgate’s quarterly net loss attributable to shareholders was $28.8 million, an improvement over a net loss of $94 million a year earlier, as its television division posted a decline in revenue and profit.

As of June 30, Lionsgate had $425.8 million in cash and equivalents and total debt of $1.9 billion.

Meanwhile, in 2024, Legendary bought out the stake Chinese conglomerate Dalian Wanda Group owned in the company . The pact left Legendary and private-equity firm Apollo Global Management in control of the company. Apollo acquired a stake in Legendary in 2022 for $760 million.

Lionsgate is scheduled to release financial results for its fiscal 2027 second quarter (the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026) after market close on Thursday, Nov. 5.

title_original: Nikita Teryoshin and the imagery of protest, artwashing and political defiance with Pussy Riot
editorial_title_zh: 尼基塔·特里奥申与抗议、艺术洗白及政治反抗的影像：与 Pussy Riot 的合作
editorial_excerpt_zh: 尼基塔·特里奥申记录政治抵抗，揭露宣传与艺术洗白。从烧毁俄罗斯护照到拍摄 Pussy Riot 在威尼斯双年展上的抗议，他的作品通过强有力的影像放大了异见。

年初，在俄罗斯对乌克兰发动全面入侵之后，出生于俄罗斯的摄影师尼基塔·特里奥申受一家德国新闻杂志委托，记录乌克兰难民涌入波兰边境的情况。由于手部受伤，他被迫退出这项工作，并感到无所适从。长久以来与出生国疏离、对欧洲东部边境发生的事件感到震惊，他萌生了用相机表明立场的冲动。于是，他拿着自己的俄罗斯护照，将其贴在柏林灰蒙蒙的天空背景下点燃并拍了下来。", "translated": true}, "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "自那以后，特里奥申的个人项目探讨了全球军火贸易与战争营销、政治大会与治理机构，以及压迫性盗贼统治所采用的艺术洗白和体育洗白策略。在他烧毁俄罗斯护照的前后，他加入了一个蓬勃发展的在线 NFT 社区，并通过它接触了许多乌克兰和俄罗斯艺术家。“那种氛围极其支持，”他说，“来自世界各地的摄影师互相帮助。我想，也许我可以把这张护照照片铸造出来，为乌克兰筹集一些资金。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他铸造并售出了这枚 在柏林俄罗斯大使馆外组织的抗议活动。他拍了一些照片，事后发给了该组织。两年后——在一次前往卡塔尔拍摄该石油国首届久负盛名的商业艺术博览会“巴塞尔艺术展”（Art Basel）的迷失之旅后——特里奥申反思了艺术界如何作为地缘政治工具，服务于交织的权力和冲突领域。随后，他收到了 Pussy Riot 创始人娜佳·托洛科尼科娃（Nadya 极具数字素养，且充分意识到其（年轻的女性）身体作为一种媒体形式的政治力量，通常会在即将开展的行动前向摄影师和博主进行吹风。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
Invited to document feminist performance art collective Pussy Riot protesting the Russian Pavilion at the Venice Biennale, Nikita Teryoshin became part of the action in the wider world

In early 2022, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russian-born photographer Nikita Teryoshin was commissioned by a German news magazine to document the influx of Ukrainian refugees across the Polish border. Due to a hand injury, he was forced to pull out of the job, and was left feeling listless. Long estranged from his country of birth, and horrified by the events that were unfolding on Europe’s eastern border, he felt the urge to use his camera to make a statement. So taking his Russian passport, he held it against a grey Berlin sky, set it on fire, and photographed it.

Born in Leningrad, Teryoshin moved to Dortmund, Germany, as a teenager. His father worked as a set designer and painter for theatre and television, and the young Nikita found these studios and workshops fascinating. It was perhaps there he developed a certain sensitivity to the construction of images, the way that arrangements of objects, bodies and lighting create meaning, and the technical tricks and special effects that can confuse an audience’s sense of the real. From there he realised that, across culture, media and politics, there is almost always a ‘backstage’, a hidden space in which spectacle is carefully engineered, labour is invisibilised, and wealth and reputation are laundered.

Teryoshin’s personal projects have since explored the global arms trade and the marketing of war, political conventions and the apparatus of governance, and the strategies of artwashing and sportswashing employed by repressive kleptocracies. Around the time he burned his Russian passport, he was part of a burgeoning online NFT community, through which he engaged with many Ukrainian and Russian artists. “It was super supportive,” he says. “Photographers from all over the world, helping each other out. I thought, maybe I can mint this photo of my passport, and raise some money for Ukraine.”

He minted and sold the NFT, and printed posters and limited editions of the image, raising thousands of euros which he donated to causes in Ukraine. The photograph was published in German broadsheet Die Zeit , and circulated widely online. Some Russians mocked the burning as cowardly and superficial, enacted from the relative safety of a third nation. An old classmate of Teryoshin’s posted on social media that she had reported the image to security services and that, if he attempted to return to Russia, he would be escorted directly from the plane to a prison cell.

Teryoshin is sanguine. “From the beginning, it was pretty clear that I can’t go back [to Russia],” he says. “Before the full-scale invasion, burning a passport would have landed you with a fine. But they’ve changed the law, and applied it retrospectively, so it’s now 16 years in prison.”

“It’s absurd to say that you’re not into politics and you’re against the war, but then be comfortable going out onto a global stage and representing [the aggressor]” – Nikita Teryoshin

The photographic medium is deeply implicated in the ecologies of contemporary protest. Setting fire to passports, flags and sacred texts as an act of resistance relies on the presence of a camera for political potency and endurance. Photographs of flames seem to arrest the physics of combustion, and suggest that a fire might, in fact, burn ceaselessly. The image of Teryoshin’s flaming passport is a performance of ritualised agency that lingers conceptually, with the potential to act as a universal igniting force. And the idea that a political fire could burn forever in the hearts and minds of a population is the kind of notion that tends to trouble insecure autocrats.

After the death of Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny in a Siberian penal colony in February 2024, Teryoshin joined a protest at Berlin’s Russian embassy, organised by the dissident feminist performance art collective Pussy Riot. Taking some photographs, he sent them to the group afterwards. Two years later – after a disorienting visit to Qatar to shoot the petrostate’s inaugural edition of the prestigious commercial art fair Art Basel – Teryoshin was reflecting on how the art world functions as a geopolitical instrument for intersecting spheres of power and conflict. Then he received a message from Pussy Riot’s founding member, Nadya Tolokonnikova; the group would be staging a protest outside the Russian Pavilion during the preview week of the Venice Biennale, and they wanted him to document it. It seemed to Teryoshin like “a greeting from the universe”.

Since their formation in 2011, Pussy Riot have adopted strategies of punk spectacle and aesthetic actionism, producing pictorially intense and vivid image-acts that seem to prioritise the visual afterlife of protest over the act itself. The group emerged at around the same time as Instagram, a time when everyone from the Pope to the Israel Defense Forces was joining Twitter, and when social networks were having far-reaching off-screen sociopolitical impact (including during the Arab Spring). Highly digitally literate, and well aware of the political power of their (youthful, female) bodies as a form of media, Pussy Riot typically brief photographers and bloggers in advance of their upcoming actions.

Image production is a key component of their strategy, the group adopting hybridised radical feminist approaches to protest to explore the argumentative potential of visibility. Their brightly coloured balaclavas are an important visual motif within this strategy, and they anonymise and de-individualise group members. Pussy Riot have claimed to have dozens of members, and say that their participants can totally differ in each guerilla performance. Their headwear also creates visual parallels with other direct action, liberation and feminist movements, which have embraced the balaclava as a performative object.

The presence of Femen, which was founded in Ukraine but now operates internationally, adds a further dimension. Femen employ their own naked bodies as a form of media, forcing a confrontation with the precarity and vulnerability of the nude female form – and crucially, generating further visibility. With slogans painted across their bare breasts, Femen attempt to invert the hypersexualised connotations of female anatomy, and suggest that the body can assert its own meanings and values.

It is a strategy that has been critiqued. What Femen present as a liberated female image has been criticised as a hegemonically white, thin and able-bodied representation; the group has also been accused of prioritising a deeply Western view of female emancipation, specifically targeting Islam and rejecting women who have an alternative relationship with their bodies. Femen activists’ confrontations with law enforcement and security services make for compelling imagery, but the political meanings they produce are not always shared.

Nevertheless, as Judith Butler writes in Notes Toward a Performative Theory of Assembly , “though the body in its struggle with precarity and persistence is at the heart of so many demonstrations, it is also the body that is on the line, exhibiting its value and its freedom in the demonstration itself, enacting, by the embodied form of the gathering, a claim to the political”. Pussy Riot and Femen’s emphasis on corporeality risks reinforcing the patriarchal notion that the attention paid to women should be arbitrated by their physical appearance. However, it is worth remembering that in the Russian and post-Soviet cultural context, in which the Orthodox Church wields significant influence, the presence of non-conforming female bodies in public space can still be considered societally menacing.

“Russia wages hybrid war,” explained Tolokonnikova to the assembled press on the steps of the Russian Pavilion, as the protest was dissipating. “It’s not just tanks and drones, murders and rapes in Ukraine, but it’s also culture, art, language, so called ‘soft power’. It’s clear that it’s part of their military strategy and that’s the way they try and conquer the West. And you guys just open the doors to them,” she continued, before concluding with a weary sarcasm: “That’s funny.”

When challenged on the presence of states accused of crimes against humanity, Biennale president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco appealed to liberal false balance; “If the Biennale started selecting works [on the basis of] passports, it would cease to be what it has always been: the place where the world comes together.” It seems a platitudinal take from the conservative intellectual – and former leader of the youth wing of the neo-fascist Italian Social Movement party – confusing rogue state propaganda with artistic freedom.

Teryoshin is alive to the paradox that emerges when “the world comes together” in Venice. “I think the normalisation of Russia’s presence in Europe, in this cultural environment, is totally wrong,” he states. “People say to me, ‘Yeah, but the artists who are part of it are not into politics’. Or, ‘There is no one from Russia who is really into this war’. But it’s absurd to say that you’re not into politics and you’re against the war, but then be comfortable going out onto a global stage and representing [the aggressor]. One of the best examples of artwashing is this pavilion.”

He accepts his position as an active agent in the protest’s efficacy – especially as the Russian Pavilion was only open during preview week, when few members of the public would have been present for the demonstration. “You could say the photographs become more important than the action itself,” Teryoshin reflects. “There were maybe 200 people there at that moment. But the only thing the world will see are the pictures.”

article_text:
The Water Knows

A woman in a white dress stands at the water’s edge.

Whatever brought her there remains outside the frame. Only traces remain: an undone face, a wound, a dress whose symbolic meaning gradually seems to dissolve.

She enters the water.

A second woman appears. Friend, lover, protective presence or darker force, nothing allows her to be clearly defined. I wanted her to remain unresolved.

From that moment on, the water is no longer a backdrop. It becomes a threshold. The bodies draw closer, reflect and fragment until the boundary between presence, memory and disappearance becomes uncertain.

I chose black and white to remove the narrative’s most immediate markers and leave more room for gestures, textures, shadows and reflections. The intention is not to reveal what happened, but to photograph its aftermath and the passage through it.

When the woman re-emerges, nothing is truly resolved. We do not know what she has left behind, what she has crossed, or even whether she returns unchanged.

The Water Knows begins with a simple idea: some stories reveal themselves only through the traces they leave behind.

The water has seen everything. It says nothing.

article_text:
La 29e édition de Paris Photo se tiendra au Grand Palais du 12 au 15 novembre 2026. À cette occasion, les œuvres de 1260 artistes venus du monde entier seront rassemblées pour célébrer la photographie dans toute sa diversité.

Ce mardi 8 septembre, Paris Photo présentait la programmation de sa nouvelle édition au sein de l’auditorium du Jeu de Paume, à Paris. Cette année, celle-ci sera imprégnée des célébrations des deux cents de la photographie, qui ont commencé en ce mois de septembre. De fait, comme l’a rappelé Florence Bourgeois , directrice de l’événement, la foire internationale sera « le premier rendez-vous d’envergure internationale dans le cadre du Bicentenaire » . À cette occasion, le Centre Pompidou y présentera une centaine d’œuvres de trente artistes issus de sa collection. Parmi elles se comptent de récentes acquisitions entreprises en vue de cette exposition. L’ensemble permettra de poser un regard transversal sur le médium et de montrer ses évolutions. À cela s’ajoutera un parcours dédié au Bicentenaire, beaucoup plus large, à découvrir au détour des allées du Grand Palais. À l’entrée, les visiteurs seront notamment accueillis par une installation de Thomas Ruff , qui se distingue par son approche expérimentale du 8e art. Au gré de leur déambulation, ils pourront également contempler des images élaborées à partir des premiers procédés photographiques, tels que le calotype, le daguerréotype et le photogramme.

Panorama de la création contemporaine

Au-delà de son hommage au Bicentenaire, cette 29e édition fera la part belle à la création contemporaine. Nous retrouverons Antony Cairns et SMITH dans les projets prismes, Lara Tabet et Yasmine Chemali, les lauréates du programme BMW ART MAKERS 2026 , ou encore Mirjam Reiter, Camille Cellier, Jonas Glanz et Jinyong Lian , qui sont les quatre gagnants du prix Étudiants Paris Photo. Comme à l’accoutumée, quatre secteurs accompagneront le secteur principal. Conçu par Zasha Colah et Francesco Zanot, « Voices » s’articulera autour de la disparition, un thème qui leur est venu alors qu’ils travaillaient sur les deux cents ans de la photographie. « La disparition est ainsi devenue une idée politique » , explique la commissaire invitée. Le secteur « Digital » a été imaginé par Marco De Mutiis, nouveau curateur pour Paris Photo, qui officie habituellement au Fotomuseum Winterthur, en Suisse. S’il comporte des productions en intelligence artificielle, celui-ci montrera de la photographie pensée en digital. « Émergence », situé au premier étage, accueillera vingt projets monographiques de jeunes artistes de neuf pays différents. Enfin, le « Éditions » réunira 48 maisons d’édition et libraires spécialisés. En parallèle, le parcours Elles x Paris Photo , qui met en exergue la création féminine depuis 2018, sera toujours présent.

Des archives argentiques de l’AFP à la Fisheye Gallery

Cette année, la Fisheye Gallery exposera à Paris Photo non plus dans le secteur « Émergence », mais au cœur de la nef. À cette occasion, elle proposera un échantillon inédit des archives argentiques de l’Agence France-Presse. Au recto de ces tirages d’époque se trouve une image qui a marqué la mémoire collective tandis que, au verso, ce sont des légendes dactylographiées, tampons humides et annotations manuscrites qui témoignent du geste journalistique. En mettant en évidence la matérialité de la photographie, l’ensemble consacrera ainsi « le statut de l’ “image-objet” comme fragment tangible de l’histoire » . La scénographie s’inscrira en ce sens en privilégiant la réversibilité. Par ailleurs, jusqu’en janvier 2027, quelques-uns de ces clichés sont à retrouver dans dix-sept stations du métro parisien, dans le cadre d’une exposition RATP labellisée par le Bicentenaire de la Photographie.

article_text:
Peak TV is dead. We’ve been beyond that era for a while now, with the number of shows produced annually having dropped significantly post-Covid and post-strikes. As a result, we just had the biggest example in media history of consolidation in our industry, with Paramount merging with Warner Bros. Discovery and putting two major streaming services under one roof.

Something has to change in order to get more shows and movies to the air and to better empower creators. So some of Hollywood’s top agencies — a rare coalition that includes CAA, UTA, and WME — as well as top producers like Ron Howard, Brian Grazer, Jason Blum, Mark Burnett, Peter Chernin, and more, are teaming up with an idea to bring back an even earlier era of television.

Those top agencies and producers have formed the American Entertainment Alliance , and per an announcement in the New York Times , they are pushing for federal legislation that would require major studios — including Netflix, Disney, Amazon, and Skydance — to dedicate half of their annual content budgets to be spent on independent productions in the United States. Rather than have largely consolidated studios produce the majority of their content in-house for it to then be aired on their own broadcast networks, cable channels, or streaming services, they’d like to see at least half of that content come from production companies outside their walls.

If that were to happen, it would let the creators of the shows be the owners of what they make. And the AEA believes it would send a jolt through the marketplace, in turn creating more jobs and more opportunity.

“There are fewer people deciding what gets made and what we all see, what the consumer sees,” Bryan Lourd, the chief executive of CAA, told the New York Times. “This change that we’re putting forth would foster an environment where more things could get financed and therefore there’d be more storytellers, more jobs created. Distribution is not the issue of the future. Who finances content is the issue.”

For those old enough to remember, this would be a throwback to the days of “Fin-Syn,” or the Financial Interest and Syndication Rules of 1970. It was regulation that made it so that the three major broadcasters, CBS, NBC, and ABC, couldn’t own the shows they aired or control their syndication. They knew their shows could air on broadcast, and they could own the rights to it and decide where it was syndicated in the future. As the Times pointed out, it led to independent, creator and talent-led juggernauts like Castle Rock, Mary Tyler Moore’s MTM Enterprises, “Dallas” producer Lorimar, and many more.

But the rules were repealed in the ’90s after the rise of cable, the belief being that there was more than enough competition now for it to not be a problem. The AEA says that’s exactly when media consolidation started running rampant and has led to this moment of 41 percent fewer scripted submissions from independent producers and thousands of jobs lost.

The AEA in addition to the budgets also wants production companies to be able to own their own shows and have licensing rights. So in theory it would give a popular show another bite at the apple to sell their show again to a different streamer years down the road, or perhaps a show that got cancelled could more easily be sold and saved by another streamer.

To try and push this forward, the stakeholders of the AEA are meeting with the people who helped to draft the recent bill introduced that would create a federal tax credit for films produced in the United States . We talked before about how seismic that legislation was to finally be introduced, and it remains to be seen if it will be adopted for good after the midterms. While the Fin-Syn rules used to be regulated by the FCC, the FCC has little oversight with streaming, so the AEA is instead looking to introduce legislation.

Despite the heavy hitters, all this comes with major challenges and caveats. Not only is anything of this nature a struggle to push through this polarized of a Congress, but the studios themselves would also fight it tooth and nail, saying they need to be able to own their content and that they already buy a bunch of shows from outside sources anyway. There are countless shows and films from the likes of Imagine, Blumhouse, MRC, and others that make up the AEA that have thrived in the current ecosystem.

But a diversity of voices and more power to creators is a good thing in our book, and it’s refreshing to have such big names teaming up to fight for the little guys.

article_text:
T wo years ago, RM of the wildly popular K-pop boyband BTS was serving as a soldier in the South Korean military when he received an offer from América Castillo, a museum curator in San Francisco: would he consider an exhibition of his private art collection?

“I loved it,” said RM (real name: Kim Namjoon) at the media preview of RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me , a new exhibition that opened in San Francisco earlier this month and is co-curated by SFMOMA’s Castillo and Hyoeun Kim. “There aren’t many things that show a person more honestly than a collection they’ve built over a long period of time.”

The result is a multi-dimensional exhibition of 142 works of RM’s private collection of mostly Korean works, including paintings, calligraphy, sculpture and even a Pokémon animation cel, in conversation with 36 of the museum’s pieces. The show has been a blockbuster success, with over 66,000 tickets sold and advance sales that were six times higher than any previous exhibition at the museum.

RM has been an evangelist for modern Korean art: a song from his 2022 solo album Indigo samples a conversational snippet from the Korean painter Yun Hyong-keun. At the SFMOMA show, Yun’s monochrome Umber-Blue sits juxtaposed next to Mark Rothko ’s No. 24 in the show. There’s also an audio guide and playlist by RM.

“I’ve always dreamed of seeing different places, times, boundaries and backgrounds all mixed together in harmony,” RM said at the preview, before adding lightly: “It could be a mess – I never formally studied art history, and I’m not a curator.

“Sometimes an outsider can bring in a new breeze,” he added.

While his celebrity looms large over the show, the collection and the curation of the show are formidable. In South Korea, gallery owners and art dealers who have met RM have told me their nickname for him is “bakhsa” (professor) owing to the depth of his knowledge. “It is especially meaningful to bring the depth and richness of his collection to a wider audience,” says Kim, assistant curator of painting and sculpture.

Some of the art is displayed with a scholarly arc, while other curation feels more intuitive. One room is titled “I Don’t Know, But I Like It.”

“I started this with an innocent heart,” RM said at the preview. “I just didn’t know that this innocence would eventually make me write, erase and rewrite hundreds of labels.” His text that accompanies the pieces combines historical context with diaristic personal reflections, in a break from museum convention.

In a placard that accompanies a Lee Ungno painting of the Gwangju uprising in 1980, a brutal crackdown on protesters by a military dictatorship, RM writes: “He painted these crowds until the day he died. Strange, isn’t it. These people are not falling. Arms raised, legs wide, they are dancing.”

Last year, as US museums grappled with the lingering effects of the pandemic on attendance, funding challenges under the current administration and lower tourism rates in many cities, SFMOMA laid off 7.5% of its workforce amid a $5m deficit. Its new director Christopher Bedford wrote that the museum would adjust its programming and budget to reflect “a reduced annual attendance normal in the range of 600,000 visitors”.

Since the RM show opened, the museum has seen an undeniable financial boost. Its success, and whether it ushers in a direction toward celebrity exhibitions, is something officials and other museums seem to already be considering. In 2024, Brooklyn Museum staged a major exhibition showcasing the private collection of Swizz Beatz and Alicia Keys, while other recent shows have focused on art made by musicians like Jack White and Paul McCartney .

Yet the dedication of BTS fans, who call themselves Army, may prove to make this show a one-off. On the day of the media preview and opening reception, a couple hundred fans lined up outside the museum entrance, one holding a sign saying she came from London for RM. Another handed journalists small bags of gifts including custom-made bookmarks, key chains and cake pops along with thank you notes for covering the exhibition.

Exhibition merch available at the SFMOMA Museum Store and web store sold out within three hours. “It’s different in so many ways,” store director Shane Salvata says of the exhibition, adding that it is important for visitors to commemorate “how special it is that he curated this show”.

“It’s unlike anything we’ve ever experienced, and probably will experience ever again,” he says.

For Castillo, who originally conceived the show, success has a different measure. “To actually see it in the galleries … people are crying in front of you,” she says. “You’re never going to expect that. It’s a beautiful surprise.”

RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me is on view at SFMOMA until 7 February 2027
